## Coordinate Geometry

While @eq-lincov stays the same, the STM $\mathbf{\Phi}$ changes depending on the state representation we choose --- 
as well as its ability to accurately capture the nonlinear dynamics present in orbit. As mentioned above, we will take two different state representations: a RIC framework
framework using CW-equations and an orbital parameterization using ROEs.

### Clohessy Wiltshire STM

To understand how $\mathbf{\Phi}$ is formed using the CW-equations, we must first visit the RIC frame. This is because the CW equations are defined in the RIC frame, which is 
fixed to the Chief satellite as shown in @fig-RIC_frame.

![Chief-Deputy RIC Frame Geometry. *Diagram generated with Gemini.*](images/RIC_frame_CW.jpg){#fig-RIC_frame width="80%" fig-align="center"}

The radial unit vector is defined by @eq-Radial.

$$
\hat{R} = \frac{\mathbf{r_c}}{||\mathbf{r_c}||}
$$ {#eq-Radial}

Where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of the satellite in the ECI frame, and the subscript c denotes the chief satellite. The Cross-Track unit vector is then defined in @eq-Cross.

$$
  \hat{C} = \frac{\mathbf{r_c}\times\mathbf{v_c}}{||\mathbf{r_c}\times\mathbf{v_c}||}
$${#eq-Cross}

Where $\mathbf{v}$ is the satellites velocity vector in the ECI frame. With the Radial and Cross-Track directions defined, the In-Track direction is defined as 

$$
  \hat{I} = \hat{C} \times \hat{R}
$${#eq-IN}

By assuming that the Chief satellite is in a circular orbit, and that the distance 
between the Chief and Deputy is much smaller than the Chief's orbital radius ($||\delta \mathbf{r}|| << \mathbf{r}_c$),
Clohessy and Wiltshire formulated the following equations.<sup>[1](#ref-cw)</sup>

The CW (Clohessy Wiltshire) equations assume the Chief satellite is in a circular orbit.
